phases.title: The 7 October attack
phases.sum: Hamas and other armed groups from Gaza broke into southern Israel, killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the deadliest day in Israel's history.
phases.detail:
The attack: Early on Saturday 7 October 2023, a Jewish holiday, Hamas fired thousands of rockets at Israel while gunmen crossed the Gaza fence at dozens of points by land, by paraglider and by sea. They attacked more than 20 Israeli communities, army posts and the Nova music festival near Re'im. Hamas called the attack 'al-Aqsa Flood', after the mosque on the Temple Mount (background: see the explainer Jerusalem and the Temple Mount status quo).

The dead: By Israel's count about 1,200 people were killed, most of them civilians, including 364 at the Nova festival. Kibbutzim such as Be'eri, Kfar Aza and Nir Oz lost a large share of their residents.

Hostages: 251 people, Israelis and foreign nationals, from infants to people in their eighties, alive and dead, were taken into Gaza.

Israel's response: On 8 October Israel's security cabinet formally declared war, and the army began the campaign it named Swords of Iron, with heavy air strikes on Gaza and a call-up of about 300,000 reservists. Hezbollah began firing at northern Israel the same day.

phases.title: The ground operation in northern Gaza and the November truce
phases.sum: Israel sent ground forces into northern Gaza and cut the Strip in two. A week-long truce in late November freed 105 hostages in exchange for 240 Palestinian prisoners.
phases.detail:
Evacuation: On 13 October 2023 the IDF told about 1.1 million people in northern Gaza to move south of Wadi Gaza.

Ground operation: Ground forces entered northern Gaza on 27 October and by early November had encircled Gaza City and cut the Strip in two along the line that became the Netzarim corridor. On 15 November troops entered al-Shifa hospital, which Israel said Hamas used as a command centre.

The truce: A truce mediated by Qatar, Egypt and the US ran from 24 November to 1 December 2023. Hamas released 105 hostages (81 Israelis and dual nationals, 23 Thais and one Filipino), and Israel released 240 Palestinian prisoners, all women and minors. Fighting resumed on 1 December after the truce broke down.

Court case: On 29 December South Africa filed a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice; on 26 January 2024 the court ordered provisional measures but did not order a halt to the fighting. Israel rejected the charge.

phases.title: Khan Younis and Rafah
phases.sum: The fighting moved south to Khan Younis and then to Rafah, where Israel took the border with Egypt. Four hostages were rescued alive from Nuseirat in June.
phases.detail:
Khan Younis: From early December 2023 the IDF fought in Khan Younis, where Israel believed Hamas's leaders were hiding. The 98th Division left the city on 7 April 2024.

UNRWA: In January 2024 Israel said 12 UNRWA staff took part in the 7 October attack. Several donors paused funding, and a UN inquiry later found that nine staff may have been involved; they were fired.

Rafah: On 6 May 2024 Israel began its operation in Rafah, where about a million displaced people had gathered, and on 7 May it took the Gaza side of the Rafah crossing. By the end of May the IDF said it controlled the whole Philadelphi corridor, the 14 km strip along the Egyptian border.

Rescues: On 8 June 2024, in Operation Arnon, Israeli forces rescued four hostages alive (Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov and Shlomi Ziv) from Nuseirat.

Hamas leaders: On 13 July an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi targeted Hamas's military chief Mohammed Deif; Israel confirmed his death on 1 August. On 31 July Hamas's political leader Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran. On 6 August Hamas named Yahya Sinwar as its new leader.

The toll: On 15 August 2024 Gaza's Hamas-run Health Ministry said more than 40,000 people had been killed. It does not separate fighters from civilians.

phases.title: Philadelphi, Netzarim and the killing of Sinwar
phases.sum: Talks stalled over whether Israel would hold the Philadelphi and Netzarim corridors. Six hostages were murdered in a Rafah tunnel, and Yahya Sinwar was killed in Rafah on 16 October 2024.
phases.detail:
The corridors: Through the summer of 2024 the main dispute in the talks was Israel's demand to keep forces on the Philadelphi corridor and to check people returning north through the Netzarim corridor.

Six hostages: On 1 September 2024 the IDF recovered the bodies of six hostages (Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Eden Yerushalmi, Ori Danino, Alex Lobanov, Carmel Gat and Almog Sarusi), murdered by their captors in a tunnel in Rafah shortly before troops reached them. Mass protests followed in Israel.

Sinwar: On 16 October 2024 an IDF patrol in Tal al-Sultan, Rafah, killed Yahya Sinwar in a chance encounter. Hamas did not name a single successor and was run by a leadership council.

Jabalia: From 6 October 2024 the IDF fought again in Jabalia and the far north of Gaza, saying Hamas had regrouped there.

UNRWA: In October 2024 the Knesset passed two laws banning UNRWA from operating in Israel and cutting contact with it. They took effect on 30 January 2025, and UNRWA's foreign staff left East Jerusalem.

ICC: On 21 November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu, Yoav Gallant and Mohammed Deif. Israel rejected the court's authority.

phases.title: Judea and Samaria
phases.sum: Attacks from Judea and Samaria rose after 7 October, and Israel answered with raids and, from January 2025, Operation Iron Wall in the northern camps. Extremists' violence against Palestinians drew sanctions from the US, the EU and the UK.
phases.detail:
Attacks: Shooting, stabbing and car-ramming attacks continued through the war. On 1 October 2024 two gunmen from Hebron killed seven people in Jaffa. On 8 September 2025 two gunmen from the Ramallah area killed six people at Ramot Junction in Jerusalem.

Iron Wall: On 21 January 2025, two days after the Gaza ceasefire began, the IDF and the Shin Bet launched Operation Iron Wall in the Jenin camp, extending it to Tulkarm and Nur Shams on 27 January. On 23 February 2025 tanks were sent to Jenin for the first time since 2002. Israel took full control of the three camps; UNRWA says more than 40,000 people were forced from their homes. Defense Minister Israel Katz said forces would stay in the camps at least until the end of 2025. On 26 November 2025 a separate operation began in Tubas, Tammun and al-Far'a.

Extremists' violence: Attacks by Israeli extremists on Palestinian villages rose. On 1 February 2024 the US imposed sanctions on violent Israeli citizens by executive order; President Trump revoked the order on 20 January 2025. The UK and the EU imposed their own sanctions in 2024.

Policy: In August 2025 Israel advanced building in the E1 area east of Jerusalem. In September 2025 the UK, Canada, Australia, France and other states recognised a State of Palestine; Israel rejected the moves.

phases.title: The January ceasefire
phases.sum: A three-stage deal stopped the fighting for two months; 33 hostages came home in its first stage in exchange for about 1,800 Palestinian prisoners. Talks on the second stage failed.
phases.detail:
The deal: Israel and Hamas accepted the deal on 15 January 2025; it was signed on 17 January and took effect on 19 January. At that point Gaza's Hamas-run Health Ministry said more than 46,000 people had been killed.

Hostages: In the first stage Hamas released 33 Israeli hostages, 25 alive and 8 dead, and separately five Thai citizens. Releases were staged at public ceremonies in Gaza. In late February the bodies of Shiri Bibas and her sons Ariel and Kfir were returned; Hamas first handed over another body in place of Shiri's.

Prisoners: Israel released about 1,800 Palestinian prisoners and detainees in return. On 22 February Israel held back 620 releases in protest at the ceremonies.

Withdrawal: The IDF left the Netzarim corridor on 9 February, and hundreds of thousands of people returned to northern Gaza.

The breakdown: The first stage ended on 1 March without agreement on the second. On 2 March Israel stopped all aid entering Gaza after Hamas rejected a proposal to extend the first stage.

phases.title: The war resumes: Gideon's Chariots and the GHF
phases.sum: Israel resumed strikes on 18 March and in May launched Operation Gideon's Chariots to take more ground. A new US- and Israel-backed body, the GHF, began handing out food at a few large sites.
phases.detail:
Resumption: On 18 March 2025 Israel launched a wave of air strikes across Gaza; Gaza's Hamas-run Health Ministry said more than 400 people were killed that day. Ground forces retook the Netzarim corridor and expanded buffer zones.

Gideon's Chariots: The security cabinet approved a wider operation in early May, and Operation Gideon's Chariots began on 16 May 2025, aiming to take and hold large parts of the Strip and push Hamas to free the hostages.

Aid: Israel let aid back in from 19 May after 11 weeks. On 26 May the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), backed by the US and Israel and guarded by US private contractors, opened its first sites in the Rafah area, bypassing the UN. Many Palestinians were killed near the sites and on the roads to them; Israel and the GHF disputed many of the reports.

Hostages: On 12 May Hamas freed Edan Alexander, an Israeli-American soldier, after direct talks with the US.

Iran: From 13 to 24 June 2025 Israel and Iran fought a 12-day war, and the US struck Iran's nuclear sites on 22 June.

phases.title: The Gaza City operation
phases.sum: Israel decided to take Gaza City and sent ground forces in from mid-September. In Doha, an Israeli strike targeted Hamas's leaders.
phases.detail:
The decision: On 8 August 2025 Israel's security cabinet approved a plan to take Gaza City. On 20 August Defense Minister Katz approved the plan, named Gideon's Chariots II, and about 60,000 reservists were called up.

Famine report: On 22 August 2025 the UN-backed IPC said famine was taking place in Gaza Governorate. Israel and COGAT rejected the finding and its method.

Doha: On 9 September 2025 Israel struck a building in Doha where Hamas's negotiating team, including Khalil al-Hayya, was meeting. The leaders survived; several others were killed, among them a Qatari security officer. Netanyahu later apologised to Qatar.

Ground operation: The ground operation in Gaza City began on 16 September 2025. Hundreds of thousands of residents moved south. The operation ended with the ceasefire of 10 October.

phases.title: The Trump plan and the October ceasefire
phases.sum: President Trump's 20-point plan led to a ceasefire on 10 October 2025. All 20 living hostages came home on 13 October, and the IDF pulled back to the 'yellow line', still holding about 53% of Gaza.
phases.detail:
The plan: On 29 September 2025 Trump presented a 20-point plan at the White House with Netanyahu: an end to the war, the return of all hostages within 72 hours, Hamas's disarmament, a Palestinian technocratic committee under a 'Board of Peace' chaired by Trump, and a temporary International Stabilization Force (ISF). On 3 October Hamas agreed to free the hostages and hand over Gaza's administration, but did not agree to disarm.

The ceasefire: The first stage was agreed in Egypt on 8–9 October, and the ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025. The IDF withdrew to the 'yellow line'.

Hostages and prisoners: On 13 October Hamas released all 20 living hostages. Israel released about 1,968 Palestinians: 250 prisoners serving long sentences and about 1,700 Gazans held since the war began. The bodies of the dead hostages were returned slowly over the following months; the last, police officer Ran Gvili, was recovered by the IDF on 26 January 2026.

Attacks: On 19 October 2025 two soldiers were killed in Rafah and Israel struck back across Gaza; on 28 October another soldier was killed and Israel struck again.

The UN: On 17 November 2025 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the plan, the Board of Peace and the ISF until the end of 2027.

now.title: The second stage: Board of Peace, ISF and disarmament
now.sum: The Board of Peace and a Palestinian technocratic committee were set up, and Hamas agreed in July to a disarmament roadmap, but Israel has not accepted it and still holds more than 60% of Gaza. The PA held local elections and has set general elections for 11 September 2027.
now.detail:
Second stage: US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the start of the plan's second stage on 14 January 2026. The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a Palestinian technocratic body headed by Ali Shaath, was announced the same week. On 22 January Trump signed the Board of Peace charter at Davos with about 20 other leaders; Nickolay Mladenov is its High Representative for Gaza. After the last hostage's body was recovered, Israel reopened the Rafah crossing on 1–2 February for a limited number of people, with EU monitors.

ISF: In February the ISF commander, US Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers, said Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Albania had committed troops, toward a planned force of 20,000 that would start in Rafah. Deployment slipped. On 26 July Israel's cabinet approved the entry of up to 200 ISF troops; Uganda's parliament approved sending troops in August.

Disarmament: On 30 July Hamas accepted a Board of Peace roadmap to hand over its police weapons and then heavy weapons and tunnels in step with Israeli withdrawals; Trump announced it on 31 July. Netanyahu said on 4 August that Israel had not agreed, and the Board said Israel would not leave the area beyond the yellow line before disarmament. Israel, which held about 53% of Gaza at the ceasefire, now holds more than 60%. In late August Mladenov told the Security Council both sides were failing their obligations.

Attacks and strikes: Attacks on troops and Israeli strikes continued. By 17 June 2026 Gaza's Hamas-run Health Ministry said 1,005 people had been killed since the ceasefire, and 73,001 since October 2023. The war with Iran that began on 28 February 2026 also drew attention away from Gaza.

Palestinian politics: Municipal elections were held on 25 April 2026, including in Deir al-Balah, the first vote in Gaza since 2006 (turnout there 22.7%). Fatah's 8th conference, its first since 2016, met on 14–16 May and re-elected Mahmoud Abbas. Hamas chose Khalil al-Hayya as its Gaza head in May and as head of its political bureau on 20 July, defeating Khaled Meshaal. On 10 October Abbas postponed the legislative vote set for 28 November 2026 and set presidential and legislative elections for 11 September 2027.

Judea and Samaria: On 8 and 15 February 2026 Israel's cabinets approved opening the land registry and registering land in Area C. The EU (11 May) and the UK, Canada, France, Australia, New Zealand and Norway (9 June) imposed new sanctions over extremists' violence; Israel rejected them.
